pr_title: Bluetooth: audio: hap_harc: Add HAP Hearing Aid Remote Controller role support
pr_body:
This PR adds HAP Hearing Aid Remote Controller implementation along with unit tests, bsim tests and shell commands. The changes include HAS Client implementation refactor and functionality extension (incl. Write Preset Procedure, handling Hearing Aid Features notifications).

Fixes https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/60861
fixes https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/44056

review_comments:
HARCs are not part of sets, so this is a confusing name. 

Suggest to just rename to
```suggestion
/* Hearing Aid Controller Maximum Set Size */
#define BT_HAP_SET_SIZE_MAX 2
```

I understand why you do this, but this if effectively disregarding the behavior of the GATT layer, which also means that if that GATT layer change behavior, that behavior need to be copied here, since you are not relying on the API (callback). 

It's unlikely to be an issue, but it also does not feel like the right approach - Although on the other hand it's not much different than just ignoring the callback when it's being unsubscribed, so it is OK to keep as is.
Does this need to be thread-safe?

I am not sure. Can you elaborate, i.e why this particular operation? The callback is ran from cooperative thread, and I think there is assumption that the Bluetooth API in general has to be called from cooperative thread as well.

`bt_has_client_bind` calls `inst_alloc` which also copies an address to `&inst->addr`, so we have a public API function that modifies the same value as this callback does, with a non-atomic operation. 

It's very unlikely to be an issue, so it's OK as is I think
IMO when we return an error code in a function, it doesn't make sense to also log it as an error
But the return code is the same, so I think it gives additional information which parameter is invalid
Agreed, but I would suggest to use `LOG_DBG` in that case

The term or concept of `bind` does not really exist anywhere else in Zephyr, and it is not explained here what it means. 

Can you elaborate? Is this an alternative to the `discover` functions we have for other profiles?

Yes, I broke the compatibility with other profiles by adding the `bind`/`unbind` functions.
The reason is there's a need to give application possibility to clear (unbind) the instance. That includes GATT subscription removal and removal of service-related persistent storage.

> That includes GATT subscription removal 

Why is that a useful feature?

> removal of service-related persistent storage.

You could argue that removing the bond for the device should remove this information, similar to how we handle keys. With this approach, when removing a bonded device, we would have to call the `_unbind` for each profile that implements it. The profile implementation could use the `bt_conn_auth_info_cb.bond_deleted` callback to trigger this behavior; unless you have some other usecase in mind where you'd only want to clear e.g. HAP data?

IMO, Ideally, the application should not be bothered with these details.  However, I can also see how ownership of persistent storage might lie with the application, which might require an application level cleanup.  Is this something we can fix in a subsequent PR?

> However, I can also see how ownership of persistent storage might lie with the application, which might require an application level cleanup. Is this something we can fix in a subsequent PR?

That should be done via a callback if it is needed IMO
When can this happen?

It happens when the notification is received before the application is notified about the service connection, i.e. the HAS has not been subscribed for all characteristics (so the discovery/connection procedure has not been completed yet).

If we aren't subscribed, then why would we receive the notification? 

Isn't this already done in GATT in `bt_gatt_notification` where notifications for unsubscribed handles are ignored?
What is the purpose of having this as a separate struct from `struct bt_hap_harc_cb`?

While multiple application modules might be interested in profile connection related callbacks (that's why I implemented `bt_hap_harc_cb` as callback list), `bt_hap_harc_preset_cb` the preset related callbacks, will be probably registered once by application module that caches (or not) the presets. The HAP HARC implementation does not define the size of cache, thus it's up to implementation whether it stores all of the presets read, or just a subset of it (that are specific to some scenario or vendor defined etc).
What is the advantage of using bubblesort over qsort, since you replaced it?

It's because `qsort` does not allow to pass `user_data`, like `struct bt_csip_set_coordinator_set_info *` in this case.
As the existing `active_members_store_ordered` stores the `info` in global `active` context variable, I could not call this function. Thus I added custom sorting function that has `const struct bt_csip_set_coordinator_set_info *info` as one of the parameters and can be used outside as well.

I enclosed my motivation in commit message:
```
The function implements bubble sort in place so that is able to compare the ranks without a need to store the set_info in static global variable.
```

Can't we use `qsort_r` for this instead?
From the `qsort` manpage:

> The qsort_r() function is identical to qsort() except that the comparison function compar takes  a  third argument. A pointer is passed to the comparison function via arg.  In this way, **the comparison function does not need to use global variables to pass through arbitrary arguments**, and is therefore reentrant and safe to use in threads.
Can you add a `hap.rst` next to the other shell documentation files with a brief explanation on how to use (at least some of) these commands?
Should just be `enum harc_flag`

When is this run? 

Is `inst->err` set if disconnected?

Providing the callback in the parameters is not necessarily better or worse than the approach we've otherwise taken with most profiles, but it's certainly different :)

It has some advantages, but also disadvantages. 

Can you elaborate on why you went with this direction, rather than the one we've more commonly used in LE Audio?

That is a fair argument. This approach is also similar to the GATT API. 

The downside of this approach, is that for applications that do not have dynamic memory management (e.g. to be MISRA compliant), it also means additional memory usage, as the parameters need to be `static`ally allocated, rather than stack allocated, as they need to valid until the end of the procedure, so you have a permanent increase in memory usage. If you want to handle multiple devices at the same time, that memory increase is linear to the number of connections you support (e.g. what we have for multiple client implementations that use an array of `[CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN]` for the GATT parameters. 

The approach with the callback in the parameters, rather than a pre-registered one, also have a few other advantages from a developer perspective, so it's not a bad approach as long as you've come to terms with the (potential) increase in memory. 

That being said, I would prefer to use the same approach for all LE Audio APIs, so currently I would suggest going with the approach we use for the other profile implementations, and then set up a discussion to determine which approach is most suitable, and apply that across the LE Audio stack. (I'm a sucker for consistency).
We should unref the `conn` here

`that has been deleted.`
But the callback is called `remove`. 

It is unclear to me whether this is supposed to tell the application to remove something, or tell the application that something has been remove**d** (or deleted).

It tells the application that something has been removed on the HAS Server, thus the app is obliged to remove the cached entry (if stored).

The callbacks are named like this because I wanted them to look like operations on some preset cache list.
So if something has been changed on remote, the stack instructs the app to apply the changes on local cache.

Right. I'd perhaps modify the text to reflect that more explicitly:

"index that has been deleted on the remote server." so it doesn't indicate that something locally has already been removed.
Given that you store the ID as well, don't we need to include the `id` when doing this lookup?
Ditto for the `inst_alloc` below

Unsure I understand what this does. 
Is this the opposite to `remove`?
Yes, this application callback is called to request the app to store the preset record (or update the existing entry if it's already there)

Alright, that makes sense. Not completely sold on the naming of this function though. 

Since it's handling a notification/read of a preset, maybe `(*preset)` could work? Or is that too generic? 

I would also be OK with the current name, so not a blocker.

I'm a bit confused about this. 

What is a set ID? 
Why is the conn_index being assigned it? Isn't that pretty much the opposite of a set ID?

It's used to pair the devices. So the devices with the same `set_id` value are known to be in set.
The devices that are not in set will just have `set_id` value == bt_conn_index.

Maybe it's just because I can't find it in the GH code browser, but I don't see `set_id` being assigned to anything but `harc->set_id = conn_index;` in `bt_hap_harc_bind` and then with `harc_1->set_id = harc_0->set_id;` in `harc_set_add`, but if `harc_0->set_id` is always the `conn_index` then it's equally confusing.
